record.original_question: Does every graph that triangulates a surface have a homeomorphically irreducible spanning tree?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 4.9 Every graph that triangulates some surface has a homeomorphically irreducible spanning tree.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A homeomorphically irreducible spanning tree (HIST) of a connected graph $G$ is a spanning tree of $G$ that contains no vertex of degree exactly $2$. A graph $G$ is said to triangulate a (closed) surface $\Sigma$ if $G$ can be embedded in $\Sigma$ in such a way that every face of the embedding is bounded by a $3$-cycle of $G$.

Prove or disprove: every graph that triangulates some closed surface admits a homeomorphically irreducible spanning tree.
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture (attributed to Archdeacon, originating as a question of Albertson–Berman–Hutchinson–Thomassen) that every graph triangulating a surface has a HIST is reported as confirmed: it follows from the result that every connected, locally connected graph with more than 3 vertices contains a HIST (since triangulations are locally connected). Related results (e.g., HISTs in triangulations with large representativity by Ellingham et al., and HISTs in locally connected graphs) appear in the literature supporting this resolution.

status_evidence.title: Homeomorphically irreducible spanning trees in locally connected graphs
status_evidence.snippet: Every connected, locally connected graph with more than 3 vertices contains a HIST, which confirms a conjecture that every graph triangulating a surface has a HIST.
status_evidence.claim: Surface-triangulation HIST conjecture is confirmed via locally connected graphs result.

status_evidence.title: HISTs of triangulations on surfaces
status_evidence.claim: Triangulations on surfaces are known to contain HISTs.
